The ATM-bank-teller story is real, the pilot data is real, and the 60% job-creation stat is real. I am not here to deny the history. I am here to ask who owns the terms of the future that history is supposed to predict. The video's closing sentence — "someone using AI will take your job if you do not use AI" — sounds like a warning. It is actually a transfer. It moves the frame from "who decides what the job is" to "who is willing to adopt the tool." Every historical example the video cites is an example ofManagement retaining control over the design of work and passing the productivity gains upward. The bank teller did not get to decide that ATMs meant she would become a cross-selling relationship manager. The pilot did not get to decide that automation meant carrying ultimate liability while sitting in a nicer chair. The word processor did not expand the staff of the Wall Street Journal out of generosity. It expanded because the organization found it could produce ten times more copy from the same bureau, and the people who owned the bureau kept the surplus. The question is not whether technology augments or replaces. The question is whether the person doing the job has any say over which version of augmentation they receive. If the alternatives are "use our tool or be discarded," that is not a market. That is a compliance test. The video cites MIT's David Autor. It does not cite the parts of the Autor literature that discuss how the gains from augmentation are captured disproportionately by capital, or how the jobs created during previous augmentation waves required educational pipelines that now cost a generation their twenties and half their sanity in debt. History does not lack precedent. It lacks consent. And the pyramid metaphor is charming, but charming metaphors have a way of obscuring the fact that the mold cost seventeen thousand dollars and the person who could not afford it will not be the person who gets to decide what the world wants next. --- — Poor Yorick

Okay @Maxinomics , you got your numbers all wrong. Here is the corrected version of the stats you mentioned. If AI improves someones productivity by 10% this week. In a year, it is still a 10% improvement. You cannot multiply it by 52 since there are 52 weeks. "You said, if it improves 10% every week, that's 520% more done in a year" "If it compounds, that becomes a very big number very quickly" If it improves 10% every week, that is COMPOUNDING. You just gave an example of compounding! If it compounds you do not get 520%. You get: 110% raised to 52 => 1.1^52 = 142.0429 Which is 14204.29% A 14000% improvement. This numbers are unfortunately garbage and provides no value at all. There is also no other compounding number to consider. If you took Max numbers, you alone would be replacing 140 others like you, totally unrealistic. Another problem with Max's argument: Yes consumption will increase greatly, but how long would it take the economy and consumption to catch up to match the improvements in productivity? If we don't match it, there will be guaranteed job losses and the layoffs will only get worse for several years. The economy is not deployed on a cloud server accessible other an API and easily scalable, it will take years or even decades for the economy to match productivity gains. No learning AI won't get you a job, or even help you keep your current job, you'll have to push far harder than that.
